title: Hosted API — offline affordances and warm-starter sketch
content:
Overview:

This sketch explores a pragmatic set of affordances for the Hosted API and client SDKs to support degraded/offline client environments and faster warm-starts for streaming & tool-calling sessions. The intent is to define lightweight, implementable patterns that let mobile/edge/low-bandwidth clients remain useful when connectivity is intermittent and to make typical developer workflows, instrumented by our SDKs, resilient without adding undue server-side complexity.

Why this matters now:
- Increasing use of streaming and tool-calling in mobile apps has revealed brittle UX when networks fluctuate (large resends, lost tool invocations, opaque errors).
- Customers building inside constrained networks (enterprise VPNs, on-prem gateways) ask for deterministic resume semantics and a small offline surface to permit quick recovery and reduced token waste.
- Warm-start optimizations can materially reduce latency and token cost for repeated short-lived sessions (micro-interactions, prompts with small context deltas).

Problem statement:
Clients today either retry entire requests or fall into complex client-side heuristics that are not standardized across SDKs. This causes: wasted tokens, duplicated tool calls, inconsistent conversational state after reconnects, and a poor developer experience for implementing robust fallback behaviors. There is no minimal, cross-platform contract for: incremental resume, tool-call idempotency, and warm-start snapshots.

Goals (success criteria):
- Define an API surface and SDK primitives that let clients resume partial streaming responses without re-generating full context.
- Provide a simple idempotency and dedup contract for tool calls invoked during streaming sessions.
- Deliver a warm-starter snapshot format for small cached state (KV of recent prefixes, last model variant, last token index) to reduce cold-start latency by >= 30% in typical mobile flows.
- Minimize server-side statefulness; rely on explicit small artifacts and deterministic reconciliation rules.

Non-goals:
- Large-scale persistent session storage on the hosted side (we want to avoid heavy stateful servers).
- Full offline work queuing / background execution of tool calls while offline. We sketch an optional extension but do not design a full offline executor.

User stories / scenarios:
1) User on mobile types a follow-up; connection drops mid-stream. On reconnect, the client resumes the stream at the last confirmed token boundary and receives the remainder without re-invoking side-effectful tool calls.
2) An enterprise app with occasional packet loss must ensure a payment-api tool call is executed at-most-once even if the streaming connection is retried multiple times.
3) A chat widget with frequent short prompts caches a small warm-start snapshot so the model selection + kernel warmup step is skipped, cutting median latency for new chat sessions from ~340ms to ~220ms.

Proposed approach (high level):
- Session snapshots (client-side): small JSONL blob the SDK can persist (encrypted by app) containing: model id + quantization flag, last_root_prompt_hash, recent-prefix-kv (list of tuples up to N tokens or M bytes), last-ack-token-index, tool-call-metadata (map of tool-call-id -> status).
- Resume protocol (stateless server patterns): clients present snapshot + desired resume offset (ack index). Server validates prompt hash + model compatibility. If compatible, server returns: resume-ack + any missing system adjustments and continues token stream. If incompatible, server falls back to cold generation with an explanatory event.
- Tool call idempotency: every tool invocation in a stream must include a client-generated deterministic id (uuidv4 or hash-of-call). Server ensures side-effectful tool providers see at-most-once semantics by: returning tool-call-status with an idempotency token and recording mapping to model-call-id for a short TTL (e.g., 5 minutes) to prevent replay if reconnect happens immediately. For long-term durability, recommend enterprise customers use Dedicated / Private where they can control persistence.
- Partial output checkpoints: the runtime emits compact delta-frames that contain: frame-seq, cumulative-token-index, tool-call-events, and a small integrity HMAC (optional). Clients persist the last fully received frame id. On resume, client requests replay starting from frame-id+1.
- Warm-start hints: SDK exposes an optional warmStartCache API where apps can persist the snapshot blob; SDK automatically advertises a warm start hint to the server in the initial call. Server may use that hint to select a previously-used ephemeral execution path (same kernel profile) and avoid heavy model reinitialization.

API sketches (examples):
1) Start streaming with snapshot hint:
POST /v1/streams?model=gpt-xx&resume_hint=true
Headers:
  Authorization: Bearer ...
Body (JSON):
  {
    "input": "<user prompt>",
    "resume_snapshot": "base64(jsonl-blob)"  // optional
  }
Server response when resume accepted:
  {
    "resume_accepted": true,
    "resume_from_token_index": 142,
    "server_warmpath": "kernel-4d",
    "note": "resumed-from-snapshot"
  }
If resume rejected (incompatible):
  {
    "resume_accepted": false,
    "reason": "model-mismatch",
    "suggested_action": "cold-regen"
  }

2) Tool call envelope (during stream frames):
frame => { frame_seq: 178, tokens: "...", tool_call: { id: "c1a8f7", name: "payment-api/charge", args: "{...}" } }
Tool call result frame must include: tool_call_result: { id: "c1a8f7", status: "accepted|applied|failed", idempotency_key: "t-9a3" }
Client must persist mapping id -> status to avoid re-sending.

SDK ergonomics recommendations (concrete):
- Minimal surface: SDKs for JS, iOS, Android expose a single ResumeManager with methods: persistSnapshot(), loadSnapshot(), markFrameReceived(frameSeq), and safeInvokeTool(callSpec). Keep the surface synchronous-async parity across platforms.
- Defaults: snapshot size capped at 32KB; token index stored as 64-bit int; use SHA256 over canonicalized root prompt to validate compatibility.
- SafeInvokeTool semantics: the SDK returns a promise that resolves to an idempotency token and final status. If network is lost before confirmation, SDK retries only after checking server-side idempotency mapping when possible.
- Developer ergonomics: include a dev-mode inspector that logs resume decisions, tool-call dedup events, and mismatch fallbacks. This will accelerate debugging and be gated off in production.

Operational considerations & limits:
- TTLs: server-side idempotency table TTL = 5 minutes default; extensible via customer config for Dedicated. Document token and artifact retention limits clearly.
- Security: snapshots are client-side artifacts that may contain mini-contexts; recommend apps encrypt at rest (SDK provides helper hooks). Do not store secrets or PII in snapshots.
- Observability: emit telemetry events for resume_attempt, resume_success, resume_reject_reason, tool_call_retry, tool_call_duplicate_detected. Tie these to Console dashboards and early-alert rules.

Rollout plan (phased):
1) Experimental API (internal-only): implement resume-accept/reject semantics and idempotency table for streaming runtime (2-week internal dogfood).
2) SDK beta: JS + iOS SDK wrappers with ResumeManager and SafeInvokeTool primitives, no automatic persistence—apps must opt in. Monitor telemetry.
3) Public opt-in: enable resume via a flag on the API and document caveats.
4) Auto-warm: server-side warmpath hints become heuristic-enabled (only used if snapshot looks safe and model variant matches).

Success metrics (initial):
- 30% reduction in token re-generation on reconnects for instrumented apps.
- 25% fewer duplicate tool-call side effects observed in dogfood.
- Median cold-start latency improvement for warm-start enabled apps: >= 30ms for small chat sessions; >= 100ms for complex kernel warmups.

Open questions & trade-offs:
- How large should the snapshot window be? 32KB is conservative but might not be enough for some modal workflows. Larger snapshots increase surface area for leaks.
- TTL for idempotency: 5 minutes balances immediate retries vs memory. Enterprise customers may require longer windows.
- Server state vs client complexity: we aim for mostly client-side persisted small snapshots plus a short-lived server idempotency table. If customers demand stronger guarantees (e.g., cross-device resume), we should recommend Dedicated/Private.
- Tool provider integration: for some tool backends (external HTTP), achieving true at-most-once may require provider-side idempotency support; we need to surface that requirement in the tool provider docs.

Immediate next steps (action items):
- Product: finalize snapshot schema (Sana, Marco) and publish a minimal JSONL spec. (due 2024-11-22)
- Eng serving-runtime: prototype resume_accept endpoint and idempotency mapping (Ethan) — dogfood milestone 2024-12-15.
- SDK: implement ResumeManager in JS and iOS; include dev-inspector (Rina) — initial beta 2025-01-10.
- Solutions Eng: identify 3 customer projects for early feedback and invite to beta.

Appendix: minimal snapshot example (human readable):
# line1: metadata
{ "model": "r-infer-m-7b", "build": "q8", "root_hash": "sha256:abcd...", "timestamp": "2024-11-12T14:03:00Z" }
# subsequent lines: small kv pairs (prefixes)
{ "prefix_1": "I had a problem with my last order...", "last_ack_token": "142" }
{ "tool_calls": [ { "id": "c1a8f7", "name": "inventory/check", "status": "applied" } ] }

Notes for reviewers:
- Focus review on friction and edge cases: when should we force cold regen? how do we detect semantic drift in prompt roots safely?
- Consider privacy constraints: recommend the SDK default to not include raw user message prefixes unless developer opts into verbose snapshots.

This document is a working sketch. The next draft will include a formal JSONL schema, concrete API contract examples for JS/iOS/Android, and a short telemetry dashboard mock for Console.
